table.text: The research was approved by the MIT Institutional Review Board.
At the end of each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet preferred to interact with.
Participants were then shown a new toy and asked which adult Elmo would choose to play with.

In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, each read part of a story to Elmo, and participants were asked which adult Elmo would prefer to read a new story with.
At the end of each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked playing with more.
After each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked more.
After each trial, participants were asked which adult knew the puppet's favorite toy.
In another study, participants were instructed to "think of nothing at all" for 20 seconds.

All participants had access to Wi-Fi and computers or tablets and were likely to be familiar with online testing, two-alternative forced choice tasks, the use of puppets as social agents, and culturally specific interactions in which an unfamiliar adult engages in pedagogical interactions.
Child participants were recruited and tested through Children Helping Science, an online platform supporting automated, double-blind, asynchronous testing without an experimenter present 158 .

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We treated four-and five-year-olds, six-and seven-year-olds, eight-and nine-year-olds, and adults as distinct age bins, with data collected and analyzed separately by each bin. The target sample size for each age bin was 33 participants per experiment. This sample size was determined by a power analysis for a one-sided binomial test, setting power = 0.9 to detect an effect size g = 0.25 at the standard α = 0.05. Exclusion criteria are reported in https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. A mixed-effect logistic regression predicting the choices of attentive or distracted agents from age (in months) did not explain significant additional variance (likelihood ratio test, χ 2 (1) = 3.61, p = .06) compared to an intercept-only model.
By contrast, fourand five-year-olds responded at chance (7/33 (21.2%); p = .75, 95% CI=[0.06,0.33]; BF10 = 0.095).

Exploratory analyses showed that eight-and nine-year-olds did not differ from adults (a likelihood ratio test comparing a mixedeffects logistic regression model including age group (adults vs. eight-and nine-year-olds) as a predictor to an intercept-only model, χ 2 (1) = 0.04, p = .84); six-and seven-year-olds differed from eight-and nine-year-olds.

A likelihood ratio test comparing an intercept-only mixed-effects logistic regression model to a model including age as a predictor (χ 2 (1) = 7.02, p = .008), but not from four-and five-year-olds (χ 2 (1) = 2.66, p = .10).

Six-and seven-year-olds again preferred the attentive agents (15/33 (45.5%) chose the attentive agents in both trials; p = .008, 95% CI=[0.27,0.61]; BF10 = 7.17), but four-and fiveyear-olds did not (12/33 (36.4%); p = .1, 95% CI=[0.21,0.52]; BF10 = 0.73).
A mixed-effects logistic regression including age (in months) as a predictor did not explain additional variance (χ 2 (1) = 0.65, p = .42) compared to an intercept-only model.

As in the preceding studies, six-and seven-year-olds showed sensitivity to others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation (15/33 (45.5%) chose the attentive agents in both trials; p = .008, 95% CI=[0.27,0.61]; BF10 = 7.17), but four-and five-year-olds did not (7/33 (21.2%); p = .75, 95% CI=[0.06,0.33]; BF10 = 0.095).
A mixed-effects logistic regression including age (in months) as a predictor did not explain additional variance compared to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 1.44, p = .2).

Six-and seven-year-olds selected the attended-to topics in both trials above chance (15/33 (45.5%);p = .008, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.27,0.64]; BF10 = 7.17), whereas four-and five-year-olds did not (10/33 (30.3%); p = .3, 95% CI=[0.15,0.45]; BF10 = 0.26).

Age in months did not significantly predict children's performance: a mixed-effects logistic regression including age did not improve fit relative to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 0.75, p = .39).
A mixed-effects logistic regression including age as a predictor did not explain additional variance compared to the intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 0.86, p = .35).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 188 columns across 16 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

-  We assessed AND ran 7 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).

summary_table.ethics_statements: The research was approved by the MIT Institutional Review Board.
live_data_statements: At the end of each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet preferred to interact with.
Participants were then shown a new toy and asked which adult Elmo would choose to play with.

In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, each read part of a story to Elmo, and participants were asked which adult Elmo would prefer to read a new story with.
At the end of each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked playing with more.
After each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet liked more.
After each trial, participants were asked which adult knew the puppet's favorite toy.
In another study, participants were instructed to "think of nothing at all" for 20 seconds.

All participants had access to Wi-Fi and computers or tablets and were likely to be familiar with online testing, two-alternative forced choice tasks, the use of puppets as social agents, and culturally specific interactions in which an unfamiliar adult engages in pedagogical interactions.
Child participants were recruited and tested through Children Helping Science, an online platform supporting automated, double-blind, asynchronous testing without an experimenter present 158 .
Child participants were video recorded throughout the experiment.
Adult participants were recruited and tested through Prolific.
All adult participants provided informed consent.

Consistent with the pre-registered analysis plan, our primary statistical test for each experiment was a one-tailed binomial test against chance (25%), because our hypotheses were directional (i.e., participants were predicted to prefer the attentive agent above chance).
Across experiments, participants completed two two-alternative forced-choice trials.
Participants were asked to point to the named object.
In the adult version, participants were informed that the study was designed for children aged 4-7, but that adult responses were also being collected for comparison.
In the second trial, two different agents each read different parts of Goodnight Moon to the puppet, and participants were asked which agent they thought the puppet liked reading with more.
After making their second choice, participants were asked to explain their reasoning verbally.
Participants were then asked which agent Elmo liked playing with more and indicated their choice by clicking on one of the images (therefore no need for warm-up trials at the beginning).
After the second trial, participants provided a verbal explanation for their choice and completed a memory-check question identifying which agent had looked at her phone more often.
As a final memory check, participants were asked which topic the agent paid more attention to in the second trial.
In Experiment 6, each participant completed two trials.
Then, participants were asked which agent Elmo liked more.
Participants were then asked which agent Grover liked more.
In Experiment 7, each participant completed two trials.
Then, the child participants were asked which adult knows the puppet's favorite toy.
At the end of the second trial, participants were asked a memory check question to identify which of the two agents in the final trial saw Grover's favorite toy in the box.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:7, File = c("exp1_analysis.Rmd", "exp2_analysis.Rmd", 
"exp3_analysis.Rmd", "exp5_analysis.Rmd", "exp6_analysis.Rmd", 
"exp7_analysis.Rmd", "exp8_analysis.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric"
)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `/Users/shengyi/MIT Dropbox/Shengyi Wu/MIT/research/attentionStudy/Attention-threeScenarios_like/Attention-adult-threeScenario/data/public/exp2_data_adults.csv` to `../data/exp2_data_adults.csv` (in exp2_analysis.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file. **15 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 5 ran without error, 1 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **7 scripts looked for 15 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `data/exp1_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp1_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp1_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp2_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/data_4AND5/public/exp2_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp2_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp3_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp3_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp3_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp5_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp5_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp5_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp6_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp6_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp6_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp7_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp7_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp7_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp8_data_4AND5.csv` to `code/exp8_data_4AND5.csv` for `exp8_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp1_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/exp1_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp1_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp2_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/data_6AND7/public/exp2_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp2_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp3_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/exp3_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp3_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp5_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/exp5_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp5_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp6_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/exp6_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp6_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp7_data_6AND7.csv` to `code/exp7_data_6AND7.csv` for `exp7_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp1_data_adults.csv` to `code/exp1_data_adults.csv` for `exp1_analysis.Rmd`; `data/exp2_data_8AND9.csv` to `code/data_8AND9/public/exp2_data_8AND9.csv` for `exp2_analysis.Rmd`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. info.title: Seeing without understanding? The protracted development of children's ability to use third-party attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation

Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences

text.text: Although children react poorly to inattentive adults, they may do so because their needs are not being met rather than because they understand that the adult is distracted by something else.

Given third-party observations, we find no evidence that children under six expect others to prefer attentive to distracted social partners (Exps 1-3), have preferences themselves (Exp 4), or select interventions likely to engage a partner's attention (Exp 5).

This is not due to task demands: Four-and five-year-olds have no difficulty recognizing that people prefer social partners who fulfill (versus override) their desires (Exp 6); using differences in visual attention to infer what others know (Exp 7), or distinguishing attentive and distracted social partners (Exp 8).
The results suggest that young children may understand attention primarily as visual attention rather than cognitive engagement, and thus fail to appreciate its social value.
One of the most devastating experiments in developmental psychology is also one of the most reproducible.
Take any healthy, alert baby, from the age of two months on; smile and interact with them warmly and then simply go still.
Keep your face neutral and do nothing at all.
In less than a minute, the previously smiling, cooing baby will decompensate, collapsing into fussing, tears, and withdrawal.
The classic still-face paradigm 1 attests to one of the most fundamental facts of child-rearing: Children thrive on adults' attention and suffer in its absence.
text.formatted: The classic still-face paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> attests to one of the most fundamental facts of child-rearing: Children thrive on adults' attention and suffer in its absence.

text.text: When adults fail to respond contingently to children, children show elevated physiological and psychological stress responses [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] , increased acting-out or "attention-seeking" behaviors [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] , and reduced question-asking and learning 11;14;15. Children's early sensitivity to others' attention plays a critical role in how they break into the social world broadly.
text.formatted: When adults fail to respond contingently to children, children show elevated physiological and psychological stress responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> , increased acting-out or "attention-seeking" behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> , and reduced question-asking and learning <ref type="bibr">11;14;15.</ref> Children's early sensitivity to others' attention plays a critical role in how they break into the social world broadly.

text.text: Neonates only days' old distinguish direct gaze from averted and far-away gaze 16;17 , shift their own attention in the direction of others' gaze shifts [18] [19] [20] (see also 21 ), and are more likely to recognize faces given direct than averted gaze 22;23 .
text.formatted: Neonates only days' old distinguish direct gaze from averted and far-away gaze <ref type="bibr">16;17</ref> , shift their own attention in the direction of others' gaze shifts <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> ), and are more likely to recognize faces given direct than averted gaze <ref type="bibr">22;23</ref> .

text.text: By the end of the first year, infants coordinate their attention with others', looking back and forth to a social partner and a target [24] [25] [26] [27] , directing others' attention by pointing [27] [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] and checking their caregivers' facial expression before approaching unfamiliar targets [33] [34] [35] (see 25;36;37 for reviews and discussion).
text.formatted: By the end of the first year, infants coordinate their attention with others', looking back and forth to a social partner and a target <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> , directing others' attention by pointing <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> and checking their caregivers' facial expression before approaching unfamiliar targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> (see <ref type="bibr">25;36;37</ref> for reviews and discussion).

text.text: Critically, infants are not limited to tracking attention in first-person contexts; they also track attention among third parties, although attention to third-party interactions emerges somewhat later in development.

Ten-month-olds (but not younger infants) expect people to look at their social partner in interactions and distinguish direct and averted gaze 38 ; twelve-month-olds process third-party interactions dynamically in real time, and expect others to respond helpfully to social communication (but not to non-verbal vocalizations like coughs 39 ) and older toddlers infer collaborative goals from shared social interactions [40] [41] [42] and selectively track gaze in face to face interactions 43 .
text.formatted: Ten-month-olds (but not younger infants) expect people to look at their social partner in interactions and distinguish direct and averted gaze <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> ; twelve-month-olds process third-party interactions dynamically in real time, and expect others to respond helpfully to social communication (but not to non-verbal vocalizations like coughs <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> ) and older toddlers infer collaborative goals from shared social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> and selectively track gaze in face to face interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> .

text.text: Consistent with this developmental trajectory, both neural and behavioral evidence suggest that infants increasingly attend to third-party interactions between the first and second year of life 44;45.
text.formatted: Consistent with this developmental trajectory, both neural and behavioral evidence suggest that infants increasingly attend to third-party interactions between the first and second year of life <ref type="bibr">44;45</ref>.

text.text: Toddlers' ability to engage in joint attention with their social partners supports children's word learning and communicative skills [46] [47] [48] [49] [50] [51] and becomes increasingly sophisticated over the second year of life.
text.formatted: Toddlers' ability to engage in joint attention with their social partners supports children's word learning and communicative skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref> and becomes increasingly sophisticated over the second year of life.

text.text: Two-year-olds are aware not only of what their partner is looking at but of the fact that both they and their partner are (or are not) attending to the same thing.

By two, toddlers selectively point to objects their caregiver did not see 52 and by three and four, children adjust their communication to their partners' visual access, providing more information when their conversational partner lacks visual access to a scene (e.g., shifting from pronouns to proper nouns depending on whether their partner has or lacks visual access to the referent 53 ).
text.formatted: By two, toddlers selectively point to objects their caregiver did not see <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> and by three and four, children adjust their communication to their partners' visual access, providing more information when their conversational partner lacks visual access to a scene (e.g., shifting from pronouns to proper nouns depending on whether their partner has or lacks visual access to the referent <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> ).

text.text: By three and four, children also reason about the connection between visual attention and epistemic states, expecting observers to be more likely to know information they have perceptual access to than information for which they lack perceptual access [54] [55] [56] [57] (though see [58] [59] [60] for children's failures on some variants of these tasks).
text.formatted: By three and four, children also reason about the connection between visual attention and epistemic states, expecting observers to be more likely to know information they have perceptual access to than information for which they lack perceptual access <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> (though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref> for children's failures on some variants of these tasks).

text.text: Children are also selectively likely to learn from people who are the target of others' attention.

If, for instance, bystanders attend to a person who chooses round crackers while ignoring a person who chooses square crackers, three-and four-year-olds are more likely to choose the round crackers themselves 61 .
text.formatted: If, for instance, bystanders attend to a person who chooses round crackers while ignoring a person who chooses square crackers, three-and four-year-olds are more likely to choose the round crackers themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> .

text.text: The impact of attention on children's learning also extends to third-party interactions.

Infants encode objects that are the subject of others' joint attention better than objects attended by only a single agent 62;63 and 18-month-olds (though not 12-month-olds) can use touch, in the absence of gaze, to infer joint attention 64 .
text.formatted: Infants encode objects that are the subject of others' joint attention better than objects attended by only a single agent 62;63 and 18-month-olds (though not 12-month-olds) can use touch, in the absence of gaze, to infer joint attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> .

text.text: Toddlers also learn new overheard words when speakers engage in joint attention but not when one of the third parties fails to attend 65.
text.formatted: Toddlers also learn new overheard words when speakers engage in joint attention but not when one of the third parties fails to attend <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65</ref>.

text.text: Shared attention has cognitive consequences for adults as well as children, improving adults' memory, increasing their task motivation, amplifying their judgments and emotions, and supporting learning [66] [67] [68] [69] [70] [71] [72] (see 73 for review and discussion).
text.formatted: Shared attention has cognitive consequences for adults as well as children, improving adults' memory, increasing their task motivation, amplifying their judgments and emotions, and supporting learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[66]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[71]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[72]</ref> (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref> for review and discussion).

text.text: Knowing that others are attending to the same thing impacts adults' behavior even in the absence of observable cues to mutual attention (e.g., eye gaze or the visible presence of a social partner 73 ).
text.formatted: Knowing that others are attending to the same thing impacts adults' behavior even in the absence of observable cues to mutual attention (e.g., eye gaze or the visible presence of a social partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref> ).

text.text: Adults explicitly value warm, competent social partners 74 , and attentiveness may be a strong cue to these attributes.
text.formatted: Adults explicitly value warm, competent social partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74</ref> , and attentiveness may be a strong cue to these attributes.

text.text: "Phubbing", a portmanteau of "phones" and "snubbing", has been coined to capture the ways that phones distract social partners from each other in ways that negatively impact friendships, romantic partnerships, and parent/child relationships 7;9;75-82.
text.formatted: "Phubbing", a portmanteau of "phones" and "snubbing", has been coined to capture the ways that phones distract social partners from each other in ways that negatively impact friendships, romantic partnerships, and parent/child relationships <ref type="bibr">7;9;75-82</ref>.

text.text: In short, hundreds of studies attest to children's early sensitivity to others' attention in both first-and third-person contexts and to its enduring importance in human development.
This work suggests that attention is valuable, but are children themselves aware of its value?
Note that the fact that children react poorly when their social partner is inattentive or disengaged does not in itself establish this.

Children might react negatively to inattentive social partners simply because they are not getting the warm, timely responses they want, without understanding that they are failing to get these responses because their partner is distracted and attending to something else.

To assess children's understanding of the social value of attention, we must turn to children's expectations of third-party interactions, where the value of attentiveness can be disambiguated from the value children assign to their own desires being fulfilled.

In addition to letting us de-confound the value of attentiveness from the value of getting one's own needs met, children's sensitivity to the value of attention in third-party contexts is important in its own right, with implications for the development of theory of mind broadly.
Understanding others' social preferences and interactions enables a wide range of inferences about how people will act and affiliate (see 83 for review and discussion).
text.formatted: Understanding others' social preferences and interactions enables a wide range of inferences about how people will act and affiliate (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">83</ref> for review and discussion).

text.text: Knowing, for instance, that Jane prefers Sally to Anne may enable an observer to predict that Jane will be willing to incur greater costs and accept greater risks to affiliate with Sally than Anne; indeed, even infants connect social reward to the costs and risks of actions 84 (see also 85;86 ).
text.formatted: Knowing, for instance, that Jane prefers Sally to Anne may enable an observer to predict that Jane will be willing to incur greater costs and accept greater risks to affiliate with Sally than Anne; indeed, even infants connect social reward to the costs and risks of actions 84 (see also <ref type="bibr">85;86 )</ref>.

text.text: By four and five, children use social affiliations to predict who will share resources with whom 87;88 and who will share knowledge with whom 89 .
text.formatted: By four and five, children use social affiliations to predict who will share resources with whom 87;88 and who will share knowledge with whom <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">89</ref> .

text.text: By the same token, if young children fail to recognize that others prefer attentive social partners, a large swath of the social world may remain inaccessible to them, leaving children at a loss to understand why one person seeks out, confides in, or is more generous with one person than another.

These conceptual benefits may translate into real world gains, enabling children to use what they learn from observing others' interactions to better understand and navigate their own social interactions.

If, for instance, a new child at school wants to get to know an older student named Sally, and observes that one classmate is attentive to Sally while another is not, the new child may choose to affiliate with the attentive classmate, on the grounds that Sally is more likely to be friends with her and be able to introduce them.
Indeed, children might benefit from these kinds of third-party inferences even if they do not interact with any of the parties.
Suppose for instance, that Sally is directing the school play and the two classmates give conflicting reports about a fact allegedly learned from Sally (e.g., whether the cast list has been posted).
If the child understands that Sally is more likely to have confided in the attentive classmate, the child will have access to more accurate information.

Thus, understanding the role of attentiveness in other's social preferences may have real world implications and contribute to the increasing sophistication of children's peer interactions over development (see e.g., [90] [91] [92] [93] ).
text.formatted: Thus, understanding the role of attentiveness in other's social preferences may have real world implications and contribute to the increasing sophistication of children's peer interactions over development (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[90]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">[91]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[92]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">[93]</ref> ).

text.text: In the experiments to follow, we look at the development of children's ability to understand the social value of attention from observations of third-party interactions.

In light of the vast body of evidence for children's precocious and robust sensitivity to others' attention in both first and third person contexts, we were confident that children would a) understand attentional states in thirdparty interactions; b) expect others to like attentive social partners and dislike distracted ones, and c) have the same preferences themselves.

Given evidence that four-and five-year-olds can link attention to epistemic states like knowledge and ignorance [54] [55] [56] [57] , we planned to start the study with four-and five-year-olds, and then move on to younger children.
text.formatted: Given evidence that four-and five-year-olds can link attention to epistemic states like knowledge and ignorance <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref> , we planned to start the study with four-and five-year-olds, and then move on to younger children.

text.text: To foreshadow the results, we were wrong.
Across five pre-registered experiments, we found that only children six and older expect people to value attentive social partners.
We ran three additional experiments to ensure that the results reflected a genuine limitation in young children's understanding of attention rather than task demands.
We end with some thoughts about the development of children's understanding of the value of attention and what might change from early to middle childhood.
In each of two test trials, participants observed two adults interacting with a child puppet, one after the other.
Each adult engaged in a single interaction with the puppet: demonstrating a toy in Trial 1 and reading a story in Trial 2.
One adult was attentive and the other was distracted.
At the end of each trial, participants were asked which adult the puppet preferred to interact with.
After participants made their choice in the second trial, they were asked to explain their choice (e.g., "Why did you choose her?").
See Fig. 1A.

text.text: Children may have failed to infer a preference for the attentive agent in Experiment 1 because they saw only a single interaction with each agent.

Children frequently encounter distracted adults in their real lives and may (reasonably) treat distraction as a transient, contingent feature of an interaction rather than attributing a general characteristic to the adult based on the evidence of just a single interaction.

Moreover, in general, a single example may be insufficient evidence for any inductive inference; both adults and children 94;95 draw stronger inferences from two or three examples of a concept than just one, consistent with the Bayesian size principle [95] [96] [97].
text.formatted: Moreover, in general, a single example may be insufficient evidence for any inductive inference; both adults and children 94;95 draw stronger inferences from two or three examples of a concept than just one, consistent with the Bayesian size principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">[95]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">[96]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">[97]</ref>.

text.text: Motivated by this, in Experiment 2, we show children three separate examples of each agent being attentive or distracted rather than a single interaction.

The experiment followed the same general setup as Experiment 1, except that in each trial, both adult agents had three interactions in a row with a puppet (Elmo or Grover): demonstrating a toy, reading a story, and having a conversation (see Fig. 2A).

Children's sensitivity to others' attentiveness becomes more robust in middle childhood: 79% of eight-and nine-year-olds consistently chose the attentive agent, and eight-and nine-year-olds differed from younger children but did not differ from adults.

text.text: We were surprised by four-and five-year-olds' failure to expect others to prefer the attentive agent, even given evidence that the agents were consistently attentive or distracted across three separate interactions.
One possibility is that young children distinguished the attentive and distracted adults but did not treat attentiveness as a salient factor in determining the puppet's preferences in this context.

However, abundant work suggests that four-and five-year-olds expect social group members to conform to social norms [98] [99] [100] [101] , and think that social roles and categories determine how people should behave (e.g., [102] [103] [104] [105] ).

text.text: In particular, four-and five-year-olds have expectations about sharing and comforting within intimate relationships 106 and evaluate caregivers who help and protectively hinder others from their goals 107 .

text.text: Given the centrality of caregiving relationships in young children's lives 108;109 , we speculated that four-and five-year-olds might be more sensitive to adults' attentiveness if they were in a position of choosing a caregiver for the child puppet.

To see whether evaluating the social partner in a caregiving role might facilitate children's understanding that others' prefer attentive social partners, we replicated Experiment 2, except that instead of asking children which of the two adults Elmo or Grover liked playing with more, we asked which adult Elmo or Grover would want as a babysitter.
After participants made their choice in the second trial, they were asked to explain their choice.
The results of Experiment 3 replicated the pattern observed in Experiment 2 (see Fig. 3A and 3B).

A mixed-effects logistic regression including age (in months) as a predictor did not explain additional variance (χ 2 (1) = 0.65, p = .42) compared to an intercept-only model.

Only one four-or five-year-old referred to "attention" in explaining their choice; three six-and seven-year-olds did (see Fig. 3C and https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for details).

text.text: Again, these results are consistent with an emerging but still fragile sensitivity to others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation in six-and seven-year-olds.

Six-and sevenyear-olds (unlike younger children) responded above chance, but fewer than half of six-and sevenyear-olds consistently chose the more attentive agent, and there was no reliable effect of age within this four-to seven-year-old sample.

Thus far, the results seem to be in tension with an extensive literature on young children's sensitivity to others' attentiveness in first-person contexts, raising the possibility that four-and five-yearolds' difficulties here are specific to making inferences on behalf of a third party.
Children might understand that they themselves want attentive social partners but not generalize this preference to third parties.

If four-and five-year-olds appreciate the social value of attentiveness when making a choice for themselves and fail only when making an inference on behalf of others, this would suggest that the difficulty lies in third-party attribution rather than in understanding the social value of attention.

By contrast, if children are as insensitive to others' attentiveness when expressing their own preferences as they are when attributing preferences to others, this would suggest a more pervasive conceptual difficulty in understanding the social value of attention.

Some reason to think the latter may be the case is that the extensive literature on Theory of Mind does not provide many independent grounds for believing that children make judgments for themselves of this kind that they do not make for others.
Indeed, a preponderance of evidence suggests that children can represent mental states for which they have no first-person experience at all.
For instance, studies comparing the sighted and congenitally blind suggest that understanding visual concepts is independent of first-person perceptual experience 110 .
text.formatted: For instance, studies comparing the sighted and congenitally blind suggest that understanding visual concepts is independent of first-person perceptual experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">110</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, when children represent-or fail to represent-mental states, these representations develop in tandem for reasoning about their own minds and others' (see e.g., 111;112 for review and discussion).

Thus, for instance, three-year-olds who fail to recognize that others will have a false belief about the contents of a container also fail to represent their own, immediately prior, false beliefs 113.
text.formatted: Thus, for instance, three-year-olds who fail to recognize that others will have a false belief about the contents of a container also fail to represent their own, immediately prior, false beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">113</ref>.

text.text: In Experiment 4, we test the hypothesis that young children's difficulty understanding the social value of attentiveness is specific to third-party attributions and does not extend to judgments they make on their own behalf.
Additionally, we address another potential concern with the preceding experiments.
Tracking differences of attentiveness across two identical twins might have been too cognitively demanding for the youngest children.
The twin setup may have made the characters harder to distinguish or may have drawn attention away from the subtler attentional cues.

Moreover, the youngest children might expect identical twins to be similar in all respects, reducing their tendency to differentiate between them, or they might be sensitive to family dynamics that make them reluctant to choose one sibling over the other.

In Experiment 4, we address all of these concerns by replicating the designs of Experiments 2 and 3 but using two distinct people, in each trial, introduced as unrelated individuals, and by asking children a direct question about their own social preferences at the end ("Who would you like to play with more?") rather than a question about the puppet's preferences.

As in the preceding studies, six-and seven-year-olds showed sensitivity to others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation (15/33 (45.5%) chose the attentive agents in both trials; p = .008, 95% CI=[0.27,0.61]; BF10 = 7.17), but four-and five-year-olds did not (7/33 (21.2%); p = .75, 95% CI=[0.06,0.33]; BF10 = 0.095).

Nevertheless, performance among six-and seven-year-olds remained fragile, with fewer than half consistently preferring the more attentive agent, and their performance did not differ significantly from that of the younger children.
A mixed-effects logistic regression including age (in months) as a predictor did not explain additional variance compared to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 1.44, p = .2).

Children's explanations showed a similar agerelated pattern: none of the four-and five-year-olds referred to "attention" when explaining their choices; seven six-and seven-year-olds did (see Fig. 4D and https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for details).

text.text: The results of the preceding experiments suggest that four-and five-year-olds fail to appreciate the value of others' attentiveness, given observations of third-party interactions, both when inferring others' preferences and when choosing for themselves.
However, in Experiments 1-4, we manipulated attentiveness using only differences in direct gaze and joint attention.

We expected children to be sensitive to these cues given that even infants are sensitive to visual attention, and manipulating only visual attention as a cue to attentiveness allowed us to isolate the effect of attentiveness (versus affect and other cues).

Arguably, however, differences in visual attention may have provided insufficient reason for young children to infer others' social preferences, insofar as real-world inattentiveness typically involves not only reduced direct gaze and joint attention, but also delays in contingent responding, reduced communication, and lower affect.
We were also concerned that tracking differences of attentiveness across two agents might have been too cognitively demanding for young children.
To address these factors, in Experiment 5, we introduced only a single agent on each trial.
The puppet talked about two topics (e.g., animals and sports) for equal lengths of time, alternating between topics.

The adult was consistently attentive to one topic (maintaining eye contact and responding warmly and promptly throughout) and consistently inattentive to the other (looking down at a magazine, responding less frequently and with longer delays and reduced affect).
At the end of the conversation, the adult left, and children were asked which of the two topics the puppet should talk about when the adult returned.
If children expect the puppet to value an attentive social partner, they should advise the puppet to choose the topic more likely to engage the adult's attention.

Age in months did not significantly predict children's performance: a mixed-effects logistic regression including age did not improve fit relative to an intercept-only model (χ 2 (1) = 0.75, p = .39).

text.text: Again, the absence of a significant age effect and the relatively weak performance even among six-and seven-year-olds, with only a minority of children consistently choosing the attended-to topic, suggests the protracted development of children's sensitivity to others' attentiveness in these contexts.

Given children's early sensitivity to visual attention and children's own strong reactions to adult inattentiveness, we were struck by four-and five-year-olds' consistent difficulty recognizing the value of others' attentiveness, both when choosing on behalf of third parties (Exps 1-3), when choosing for themselves (Exp 4), and when choosing interventions to sustain it (Exp 5).
Why did children struggle with these tasks?

Research suggests that online studies replicate in-person ones [114] [115] [116] [117] [118] and that the longstanding practice of using puppets to stand in for social patterns in developmental studies replicates live interactions [119] [120] [121] [122] .

text.text: However, although children's social cognition with puppets resembles their social cognition with adults, children attribute more agency and experience to peers and adults than puppets, and if anything, children treat puppets more like adults than like child peers 121 , it is possible that task-specific demands in our paradigm made it difficult for four-and five-year-olds to infer others' social preferences or track others' attention.

text.text: To investigate this, we ran three additional experiments with task demands comparable to those in Experiments 1-5.
To look at whether children could reason about bases for the puppet's social preferences other than attentiveness, we modified the paradigm used in Experiments 1-3.

At the end of each trial, each adult offered the puppet a choice between two items.
The puppet expressed a preference for one of the two items.
One adult gave the puppet the desired item; the other adult gave the puppet the other item.
After each trial, children were asked which adult the puppet liked more.
After participants made their choice in the second trial, they were asked to explain their choice.

text.text: Experiment 7 suggests that children have no difficulty tracking others' visual attention and recognizing that it is informative about what others are likely to know.
This result encouraged us to look at whether four-and five-year-olds would distinguish the attentive and distracted agents, even though they failed to infer a preference for attentive agents.
Given that six-and seven-year-olds succeeded on Experiments 2-5, we restricted this study to four-to five-year-olds.

We replicated the setup of Experiments 2 and 3; however, rather than asking children who the puppet would like playing with more or who the puppet should choose as a babysitter, we asked children: "Who paid more attention to Elmo/Grover?"

Four-and five-year-olds chose the agents who did not look at her phone as the one who paid more attention to the puppet consistently across two trials, performing significantly above chance (51.5% (17/33);p < .001, 95% bootstrapped CI=[0.33,0.70]; BF10 = 57.59).

text.text: These results suggest that although four-and five-year-olds fail to infer a preference for attentive social partners, it is not because they fail to distinguish agents who pay more and less attention.
Across five pre-registered experiments, we were unable to find any evidence that four-and fiveyear-olds themselves prefer or expect others to prefer attentive to distracted social partners.
Nor did we find any evidence that four-and five-year-olds could use others' patterns of attentiveness and distraction to select topics likely to hold a social partner's attention.
By contrast, six-and seven-year-olds succeeded in all contexts except when they observed only a single interaction.

However, even their performance was surprisingly weak: Only half of six-and seven-year-olds consistently expected others to prefer the attentive social agent, children rarely referred to attention in explaining their choice, and children's responses were not adult-like until ages eight and nine.
Collectively, the results suggest that children's understanding of the social value of attention emerges relatively slowly over development.
This finding has a number of implications for the development of children's theory of mind and social cognition broadly.

Others' social preferences are informative about a wide range of behaviors, and, as discussed, enable a wide range of context-specific inferences not otherwise recoverable from the interaction (including that, all else equal, people will be more likely to seek out, spend time with, and share resources with an attentive companion than a distracted one).
Future research should look at whether four-and five-year-olds fail to use third-party attentiveness to make these kinds of inferences as well.
The current work also raises questions about the scope of children's failure to understand the social value of attentiveness.

Do four-and five-year-olds fail not only to infer that people will prefer attentive to distracted social partners but also the range of motivations people might have for preferentially attending to one person over another (e.g., that the attendedto person is better liked, more respected, more powerful, more intimidating, talking about a more interesting topic, etc.)?
Most saliently, the current results raise the question of why children as old as four and five struggle to appreciate the social value of attention.
One possibility is that children are surrounded by caregivers who are often distracted but are nonetheless (one hopes) loving and responsive.
Given this, children may fail to treat differences in attentiveness as a reason why someone should like one agent better than another.
This is possible, but it is unclear why older children, who presumably have even more exposure to distracted adults, would expect others to prefer attentive partners but younger children would not.
A different possibility is that children represent the social value of attention, but only in firstperson dyadic contexts.
Experiment 4 shows that children's difficulties persist when they are asked to make inferences for themselves; thus, the problem does not lie merely in making inferences about others' preferences.
However, throughout these studies, evidence of others' attentiveness came from observing third-party interactions.
Arguably, children might be more likely to value others' attentiveness if they interacted with attentive and inattentive social partners themselves.

Critically, however, as discussed, first-person interactions cannot distinguish the question of whether children evaluate attentiveness and prefer more attentive agents per se or whether children simply prefer agents who respond promptly to their own needs.

(Anecdotal evidence suggests that even house cats escalate "attention-getting" behaviors when their needs aren't being met; this need not mean that cats evaluate, or even represent, the mental states of their owners.)
That said, first-person interactions provide rich information about the value of attentiveness that third-person observations do not.
Children may struggle to appreciate the value of attentiveness when they do not directly experience its payoff.

This may be especially true in contexts like the ones children observed here, where the unattended-to agent did not react with distress to being (sporadically) ignored but instead proceeded normally with the interactions.
In such contexts, young children might have insufficient grounds for making negative attributions about the inattentive social partner.
Still, we have trouble believing that the leap in inferential complexity between first and thirdperson contexts is sufficient to account for children's persistent failures here.

As reviewed, even infants and toddlers are sensitive to and selectively learn from attentive agents in third-person interactions 38;39;41-44;62-65 , children's successes and failures of theory of mind tend to apply equally to first and third-person contexts 111;112 , and children did not show even incremental improvement when asked to make judgment for themselves rather than on behalf of a third-party.
This suggests that children may struggle to understand the social value of attention for other reasons.
Many studies suggest that executive function abilities impact performance on theory of mind tasks [123] [124] [125] [126] [127] .
text.formatted: Many studies suggest that executive function abilities impact performance on theory of mind tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">[123]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">[124]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">[125]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">[126]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">[127]</ref> .

text.text: In the current study, young children might have had difficulty processing the social interaction, integrating the cues to attention, and comparing them across the two adults.
If so, children might understand attentiveness and yet struggle with task demands that enable them to reliably use it as a basis for social evaluation.
This would be consistent with a dual-systems account in which some concepts emerge early but only gradually become accessible for explicit social reasoning (e.g., 126;128 ).
text.formatted: This would be consistent with a dual-systems account in which some concepts emerge early but only gradually become accessible for explicit social reasoning (e.g., <ref type="bibr">126;128</ref> ).

text.text: Critically, however, the paradigms on which four-and five-year-olds succeeded were structurally quite similar to those on which four-and five-year-olds failed.

Moreover, in a paradigm that was identical except for the test question, four-and five-year-olds successfully distinguished the attentive and distracted adults (Exp 8) even though they neither attributed a preference for, nor themselves preferred, the attentive one (Exps 2-4).

Thus, although improved domain-general reasoning abilities might well contribute to improvements in children's theory of mind in general, there is also reason to think that children's conceptual understanding of the social value of attentiveness changes over development.
Another reason young children might have struggled here is that young children treat attentiveness as a transient behavior rather than a stable trait.

Some early work suggested that children do not appeal to stable traits as explanations of behavior until ages seven and eight [129] [130] [131] [132] [133] [134] [135] [136] [137] [138] [139] [140] [141] .
text.formatted: Some early work suggested that children do not appeal to stable traits as explanations of behavior until ages seven and eight <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">[129]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">[130]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">[131]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">[132]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">[133]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">[134]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">[135]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">[136]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">[138]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">[139]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">[140]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">[141]</ref> .

text.text: However, many of these studies gave children only a single example of a behavior.

More recent research suggests that given multiple consistent examples (as in the three interactions children observed here), four-and five-year-olds infer behaviors from traits, traits from behaviors, and treat traits as stable and predictive over time (e.g., [142] [143] [144] [145] [146] ).
text.formatted: More recent research suggests that given multiple consistent examples (as in the three interactions children observed here), four-and five-year-olds infer behaviors from traits, traits from behaviors, and treat traits as stable and predictive over time (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">[142]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">[143]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">[144]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">[145]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">[146]</ref> ).

text.text: Alternatively, younger children may have a more lenient threshold for social evaluation than older children.
In all of our studies, both adults were generally helpful, cooperative, and prosocial with the puppets.
Four-and five-year-olds might have been more inclined than older children to focus on the overall positive nature of the interactions and overlook differences in attentiveness.
However, this would be somewhat surprising given children's early and robust sensitivity to adults' attention, and their insistence on adults' undivided attention in their own interactions.

The fact that children were no more likely to value the attentive agent when making judgments for themselves than for others (Exp 4) suggests that a more pervasive difficulty with understanding the social value of attention may be at play.

Perhaps the most interesting possibility is that young children's failure to treat others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation reflects not just their failure to understand the value of attentiveness, but a different understanding of what attention means.

Instead of thinking of attention as a "mental spotlight" or a way of focusing cognitive resources, young children may initially understand attention as "visual attention", effectively equating attention with the direction of visual gaze.

This kind of understanding would permit some kinds of inferences (e.g., about the relationship between seeing and knowing) but not others (e.g., that someone who is more attentive is more interested or engaged).

Although speculative, the idea that young children may not understand attention as a way of channeling thought is consistent with decades-old research on what children understand about thinking over development.

For instance, in one study looking at whether children understand thinking as an ongoing mental process (a "stream of consciousness"), researchers asked participants whether a person who was sitting still, just waiting, "has thoughts and ideas in their head".
Ninetyfive percent of adults said "yes" but only 55% of six-year-olds, 20% of four-year-olds, and 5% of three-year-olds did 147 .
text.formatted: Ninetyfive percent of adults said "yes" but only 55% of six-year-olds, 20% of four-year-olds, and 5% of three-year-olds did <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">147</ref> .

text.text: In another study, participants were instructed to "think of nothing at all" for 20 seconds.
Adults and eight-year-olds said they had thoughts anyhow, but five-year-olds claimed to have succeeded.

Thus, although abundant work suggests that four-and five-year-olds represent the propositional content of mental states [148] [149] [150] , four-and five-year-olds may not understand either the continuous flow of thought or the fluctuating nature of attention.
text.formatted: Thus, although abundant work suggests that four-and five-year-olds represent the propositional content of mental states <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">[149]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">[150]</ref> , four-and five-year-olds may not understand either the continuous flow of thought or the fluctuating nature of attention.

text.text: Other recent research is consistent with this possibility.

Six-year-olds, but not five-year-olds, can use the relative length of time others look at a target to infer its novelty and complexity (and, conversely, use a target's novelty and complexity to predict how long others will look at it) 151 .
text.formatted: Six-year-olds, but not five-year-olds, can use the relative length of time others look at a target to infer its novelty and complexity (and, conversely, use a target's novelty and complexity to predict how long others will look at it) <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">151</ref> .

text.text: Sixyear-olds but not younger children can also use the relative duration of people's attention to a task (i.e., solving a puzzle) to infer whether they had done the task before, had memorized the solution, or were encountering it for the first time 152 .
text.formatted: Sixyear-olds but not younger children can also use the relative duration of people's attention to a task (i.e., solving a puzzle) to infer whether they had done the task before, had memorized the solution, or were encountering it for the first time <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">152</ref> .

text.text: Similarly, children's ability to identify a teacher who gives rote, versus unique, feedback as the one who "wasn't really thinking" improves from ages three to eight 153 .
text.formatted: Similarly, children's ability to identify a teacher who gives rote, versus unique, feedback as the one who "wasn't really thinking" improves from ages three to eight <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">153</ref> .

text.text: Collectively, these findings are consistent with the possibility that children may fail to understand attention as a state of ongoing thought and engagement until relatively late in development.
Supposing that an account along these lines is correct, the question of what, specifically, fourand five-year-olds fail to understand about cognitive attention remains in play.

Children might fail to understand, for instance, any or all of the following: that thinking is an ongoing mental process; that cognitive attention is a limited resource; or the range of factors (external and internal) that can affect others' attention.

Any of these failures might account for the fact that four-and fiveyear-olds can distinguish attentive and distracted agents (as in Exp 8) but fail to understand why both might not be equally emotionally available and thus desirable as social partners.

Children's failure to understand attention as cognitive attention might also explain why none of the fourand five-year-olds ever mentioned the phone (or any other aspect of attention and distraction) in explaining their choice of social partners.
As children come to understand attention as a way of focusing limited cognitive resources, they may come to appreciate its value.
There are several constraints on the generalizability of these findings.

All participants had access to Wi-Fi and computers or tablets and were likely to be familiar with online testing, two-alternative forced choice tasks, the use of puppets as social agents, and culturally specific interactions in which an unfamiliar adult engages in pedagogical interactions.
These characteristics are likely to mean that our results, if anything, overestimate children's performance relative to global norms.

Conversely, however, relative to the population we tested (see https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086 for details), children in other cultures may rely less on pedagogical instruction and be more familiar with observational learning (e.g., [154] [155] [156] [157] ); in such contexts, children may recognize the value of attentiveness at younger ages than we found here.
text.formatted: Conversely, however, relative to the population we tested (see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086">SI</ref> for details), children in other cultures may rely less on pedagogical instruction and be more familiar with observational learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">[154]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">[155]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">[156]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">[157]</ref> ); in such contexts, children may recognize the value of attentiveness at younger ages than we found here.

text.text: Moreover, our framing may not be the most insightful perspective crossculturally.

Insofar as other cultures are less likely to emphasize attentiveness or distraction per se, or to distinguish these states in social interactions, what we attribute here to a developmental shift-from four-and five-year-olds' failure to use attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation to eight-and nine-year-olds' adult-like performance-may instead reflect learning a culturally specific set of values.

Future research may shed light on whether there is a relationship between children's failure to treat others' attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation and children's understanding of the nature of attention itself.

Whatever its basis, the profound dissociation between children's understanding of visual attention and their understanding of the social value of attentiveness opens up exciting new avenues for exploration.
The current work suggests that it may take many years for children to understand how much more there is to attention than meets the eye.

text.text: Before beginning an experiment, parents or legal guardians received standardized video instructions and verification checks explaining how to position the child relative to the computer and camera and how to check the audio and volume.
Parents or legal guardians were instructed that they could repeat a question if needed but could not otherwise prompt the child or interfere with the experiment.
Child participants were video recorded throughout the experiment.
Each eligible participant received $5 USD Amazon gift card.
Adult participants were recruited and tested through Prolific.
All adult participants provided informed consent.
Each eligible participant received $5 USD for their participation.
The research was approved by the MIT Institutional Review Board.
We treated four-and five-year-olds, six-and seven-year-olds, eight-and nine-year-olds, and adults as distinct age bins, with data collected and analyzed separately by each bin.
The target sample size for each age bin was 33 participants per experiment.
This sample size was determined by a power analysis for a one-sided binomial test, setting power = 0.9 to detect an effect size g = 0.25 at the standard α = 0.05.
Exclusion criteria are reported in https://osf.io/d65qt/files/uchdk?view_only=96f0ee98f7e647c1875757b48405a086.

text.text: Experiment 1 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.8, range = 4.0-5.8 years), 33 sixand seven-year-olds (M = 7.0, range = 6.1-7.9 years) and 33 adults.

Experiment 2 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.8, range = 4.0-5.9 years), 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 7.1, range = 6.1-7.9 years), 33 eight-and nine-year-olds (M = 9.2, range = 8.0-9.9 years) and 33 adults.
Experiment 3 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 5.0, range = 4.0-5.8 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years).
Experiment 4 included 33 four-and five-yearolds (M = 4.6, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years).
Experiment 5 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.8 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 7.1, range = 6.0-7.9 years).
Experiment 6 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years).
Experiment 7 included 33 four-and five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.9 years) and 33 six-and seven-year-olds (M = 6.9, range = 6.0-7.9 years).
Experiment 8 included 33 fourand five-year-olds (M = 4.9, range = 4.0-5.8 years).

text.text: Consistent with the pre-registered analysis plan, our primary statistical test for each experiment was a one-tailed binomial test against chance (25%), because our hypotheses were directional (i.e., participants were predicted to prefer the attentive agent above chance).
Across experiments, participants completed two two-alternative forced-choice trials.

The joint probability of choosing the predicted option on both two-alternative force-choice trials by chance is 25%; thus, if significantly more than 25% of participants choose the predicted option on both trials, this indicates systematic sensitivity to the experimental manipulation rather than random responding.
These tests were conducted separately within each age bin, and we report the corresponding p-values and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals.
We additionally report Bayes factors (BF10 ) for the same binomial tests (not preregistered) to quantify the strength of evidence for or against chance-level responding.
Bayes factors were calculated using the Bayesian binomial test in https://jasp-stats.org/  160 with default priors and a directional alternative (p > 0.25).
text.formatted: Bayes factors were calculated using the Bayesian binomial test in <ref type="url" target="https://jasp-stats.org/">JASP</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">160</ref> with default priors and a directional alternative (p > 0.25).

text.text: Throughout, we interpret Bayes factors using conventional thresholds 161 : BF10 > 3, > 10, > 30, and > 100 indicate moderate, strong, very strong, and extreme evidence for abovechance responding, whereas BF10 < 1/3, < 1/10, < 1/30, and < 1/100 indicate moderate, strong, very strong, and extreme evidence for chance-level responding; values between 1/3 and 3 provide only anecdotal or inconclusive evidence.

text.text: As preregistered, we then combined data across age bins and fit mixed-effects logistic regression models with age (in months, mean-centered) as a continuous predictor and a random intercept for subjects, comparing these models to intercept-only models to assess age-related effects.
