text.text: All stimulus videos were filmed against a green wall with a white table centered in the frame.
We used two puppets, a red Elmo and a blue Grover, whose mouth movements were controlled by hand.
In each test video, a puppet was placed on one side of the table, and one agent was on the opposite side.
All experiments except Experiment 5 began with an introduction video.
In this video, the puppet was in the middle while two agents entered one after the other and stood on opposite sides, equidistant from the puppet.
In Experiment 1, Elmo served as the puppet character, and two sets of materials were used.
In one trial, the materials included a shape-sorter toy with animal-shaped blocks and a block-sorting toy.
In the second trial, the materials included a storybook containing Goodnight Moon and Harold and the Purple Crayon.
In Experiments 2, 3, 4, 7, and 8, Elmo and Grover were each used as the puppet character in one of the trials, and two sets of materials were also used.
In one trial, the materials included the same shape-sorter toy and Goodnight Moon.
In the second trial, the materials consisted of three 10 × 10 × 10 cm blocks and one 20 × 10 × 10 cm block, which were used to build either a bridge or a tower, and Harold and the Purple Crayon.
Except for Experiments 5 and 6, A phone holder was placed beside the agent's position in all trials, and each agent placed her phone on it upon entering the scene.
In Experiments 1 and 3, warm-up trials used cartoon-style images of a flower, ball, shoes, and bananas (around 500 × 500 pixels each).
In Experiment 5, a magazine was placed on the table close to the agents.
Participants saw a side view of the pages.
In Experiment 6, in the first trial, a yellow box with a white background was presented, containing two small transparent bowls: the left bowl held green grapes and the right bowl held red cherries.
A small silver plate was used to present either two grapes or two cherries retrieved from the bowls.
In the second trial, an orange box with a white background was used, containing two sheets of stickers: one with dinosaur-themed stickers on the left and one with space-themed stickers on the right.
A space sticker or a dinosaur sticker was picked by the agent and presented to the puppet.
In Experiment 7, two wooden boxes with sliding lids were used, one outlined in pink and the other in blue.
The pink box contained a yellow rubber duck, and the blue box contained a purple teddy bear.
When the lid of a box was opened to reveal its contents, a phone ringtone lasting 0.4 seconds was played.
Experiment 1 began with four warm-up trials to familiarize children with pointing at the screen.
In each trial, a puppet Elmo appeared in the center, with two familiar objects (e.g., a flower, bananas) on either side.
Participants were asked to point to the named object.
Then, a narrator explained that participants would watch Elmo meet two pairs of new friends.
Each pair was introduced as identical twins, played by the same person with different clothing and hairstyles.
In the adult version, participants were informed that the study was designed for children aged 4-7, but that adult responses were also being collected for comparison.
Each participant then received two test trials.
In each trial, participants watched a video of two adult agents interacting with the puppet one after another: one agent was attentive, and the other was distracted.

To ensure that attentiveness was the only systematic difference, we carefully matched the duration of interaction (M = 0.87 minutes in Trial 1; M = 1.00 minutes in Trial 2; < 1 s difference between agents within each trial), affect, facial expression, and conversational pace.
text.formatted: To ensure that attentiveness was the only systematic difference, we carefully matched the duration of interaction (M = 0.87 minutes in Trial 1; M = 1.00 minutes in Trial 2; < 1 s difference between agents within each trial), affect, facial expression, and conversational pace.

text.text: In the first trial, the two agents took turns demonstrating a shape sorter toy to the puppet, each demonstrating two sides of the toy.

After watching the interactions, children saw a test screen showing pictures of the two agents on either side of Elmo and heard a recorded test question asking which agent they thought the puppet liked playing with more.
Children indicated their choice by pointing.
In the second trial, two different agents each read different parts of Goodnight Moon to the puppet, and participants were asked which agent they thought the puppet liked reading with more.
After making their second choice, participants were asked to explain their reasoning verbally.
Each participant saw the attentive agent first in one trial and saw the distracted agent first in the other trial.

Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: Attentive, Distracted; Distracted, Attentive; or Distracted, Attentive; Attentive, Distracted.

Experiment 2 followed the same general setup as Experiment 1 except that warm-up trials were omitted and, in each trial, two adult agents had three interactions in a row with a puppet (Elmo in trial 1 and Grover in trial 2).

As in Experiment 1, interactions were closely matched in duration (Trial 1: M = 2.87 min; Trial 2: M = 3.00 min; < 1 difference between agents within each trial), as well as in affect, facial expression, and conversational pace.
text.formatted: As in Experiment 1, interactions were closely matched in duration (Trial 1: M = 2.87 min; Trial 2: M = 3.00 min; < 1 difference between agents within each trial), as well as in affect, facial expression, and conversational pace.

text.text: In Trial 1, each agent demonstrated a shape-sorter toy, read part of Goodnight Moon, and briefly conversed with Elmo.
Participants were then asked which agent Elmo liked playing with more and indicated their choice by clicking on one of the images (therefore no need for warm-up trials at the beginning).
Trial 2 followed the same structure: two new agents interacted with Grover by building block structures, reading from Harold and the Purple Crayon, and conversing with him.
Participants again selected which agent Grover liked playing with more.
After the second trial, participants provided a verbal explanation for their choice and completed a memory-check question identifying which agent had looked at her phone more often.
The counterbalancing procedure was identical to that used in Experiment 1.
Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the two pseudo-random trial orders used in Experiment 1.
Experiment 3 began with the same four warm-up trials used in Experiment 1 to familiarize children with pointing at the screen.
In the test trials, children were asked to point to indicate their choices.
The remainder of the experiment was identical to Experiment 2, except that the test question asked participants to choose which agent they thought should be the puppet's babysitter.
Experiment 4 followed the same procedure as Experiment 2, with two key changes.
First, instead of having the same adult play both roles as twin sisters within a trial, two distinct female adult agents were introduced as unrelated individuals.

Otherwise, their interactions with the puppets were identical to those in Experiment 2: each agent demonstrated the same toy, read the same portion of a story, and had the same conversation with the puppet (Elmo in Trial 1 and Grover in Trial 2).

The two interactions were also closely matched in duration (Trial 1: M = 2.85 min; Trial 2: M = 3.00 min; less than 1 s difference between agents within each trial), as well as in affect, facial expression, and conversational pace.
Second, at the end of each trial, children were asked directly about their own social preference ("Who would you like to play with more?"), rather than about the puppet's preference.

Again, each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: Attentive, Distracted; Distracted, Attentive; or Distracted, Attentive; Attentive, Distracted.
In Experiment 5, each participant received two trials, each involving a puppet talking with a single adult agent.
In the first trial, Elmo talked about two topics-animals and sports-in an interleaved ABAB sequence.

We opted for two examples of attentive and distracted interactions per trial (rather than three examples as used in Experiments 2-4) because we wanted to balance the inductive gain from multiple examples (most of which is gained in the switch from a single example to two examples 96 ) with minimizing task demands by asking children only to track a total of four back-and-forth interactions.
text.formatted: We opted for two examples of attentive and distracted interactions per trial (rather than three examples as used in Experiments 2-4) because we wanted to balance the inductive gain from multiple examples (most of which is gained in the switch from a single example to two examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">96</ref> ) with minimizing task demands by asking children only to track a total of four back-and-forth interactions.

text.text: The agent gave full attention to the puppet during one topic (e.g., sports) but was distracted, flipping through a magazine, during the other topic (animals).
Distracted agents also showed longer delays in verbal and physical responses (e.g., nodding) and displayed reduced affect.

The puppet speaks for the same length of time about each topic (i.e., the adult attentiveness does not, during the interaction, modulate the puppet's choice of topic), but the adult provides redundant cues that she is more interested in one topic than another.
The order of topics was fixed, but which topic received attention or distraction was counterbalanced across participants.
After the adult briefly left and returned, children were asked to choose which topic Elmo should discuss next (animals or sports) by clicking the corresponding image.
The second trial followed the same structure but featured a different puppet (Grover), a new adult agent, and two new topics (baking and taking a trip).
As a final memory check, participants were asked which topic the agent paid more attention to in the second trial.
Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the same two pseudo-random trial orders for which topic received the adult's attention as in the preceding experiments.
In Experiment 6, each participant completed two trials.
In each trial, children watched two agents-introduced as identical twins with different clothing and hairstyles-interact sequentially with a puppet.
In the first trial, both agents had a brief conversation with Elmo and then offered Elmo a choice between grapes and cherries, asking which he preferred.
Elmo always chose grapes, but only one agent gave him what he wanted.
All other aspects of the interaction, including duration (1.37 minutes each), affect, and conversation content, were matched between the agents.
Then, participants were asked which agent Elmo liked more.
The second trial followed the same structure with a different puppet Grover, two new agents, and two sticker options (space and dinosaur stickers).
Grover always chose space stickers, but again, only one agent fulfilled his desire.
Participants were then asked which agent Grover liked more.
As a memory check, participants identified which agent in the last trial gave Grover the sticker he wanted.

Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: (1) Desire fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, or (2) Desire not fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, Desire fulfilled, Desire not fulfilled.
In Experiment 7, each participant completed two trials.
In each trial, two agents (presented as identical twins) interacted sequentially with a puppet who offered to show them his favorite toy hidden in a lidded box.
When the puppet opened the box, one agent leaned forward to look inside; the other looked at her phone.
The puppet opened and closed the box twice for each agent.
A ringtone played each time the box was opened in both conditions.
Then, the child participants were asked which adult knows the puppet's favorite toy.
At the end of the second trial, participants were asked a memory check question to identify which of the two agents in the final trial saw Grover's favorite toy in the box.
Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two pseudo-random trial orders for the introduction of agents: (1) Look, Not look, Not look, Look, or (2) Not look, Look; Look, Not look.
Experiment 8 was identical to Experiment 2 with one modification: the test question asked participants to choose which agent paid more attention to the puppet in each trial.

Figure 1: Experiment 1 (A) Overview of experimental procedure.In the first trial, two adults (introduced as identical twins) took turns demonstrating a toy to Elmo.
Participants were then shown a new toy and asked which adult Elmo would choose to play with.

In the second trial, a different pair of adults, also introduced as identical twins, each read part of a story to Elmo, and participants were asked which adult Elmo would prefer to read a new story with.

Figure 5: Experiment 5 (A) Overview of experimental procedure.
In each trial, an adult listened while a puppet alternated between talking about two topics (animals and sports in Trial 1; baking and taking trips in Trial 2) in an ABAB interleaved sequence.
When the puppet talked about one topic, the adult was fully attentive, maintaining consistent eye contact, and providing warm, prompt, contingent responses.
When the puppet talked about the other topic, the adult was distracted, looking down and flipping through a magazine, responding less frequently with delayed responses and reduced affect.
The order in which the adult was attentive versus distracted to the two topics was counterbalanced across participants.
At the end of each trial, children were asked which of the two topics the puppet should talk more about.
(B) Percentage of participants who chose the more attended-to topics in both trials.
Significance indicators are based on one-tailed binomial tests (ns: non-significant; **: p < .01).
